evidence: Liv. 27.18: dōnec molliōris adscēnsūs viam invenīret
Sen. Ep. 53.4: dum per aspera ērēpō, dum viam quaerō, dum faciō
terms.comment: Livy’s phrase for finding a way up a hill; Seneca, swimming ashore, crawls over the rocks “looking for a way, making one”. Vergil’s invēnī, germāna, viam (A. 4.478) is a way out of a difficulty, not a road.

terms.gloss: keep to the way, not stray
evidence: Ov. Met. 2.79: utque viam teneās nūllōque errōre trahāris
terms.comment: Keeping to the right road once found; the opposite of losing it.

phrases.latin: eum parte dextrā tumulī circumīre dōnec molliōris adscēnsūs viam invenīret jubet
phrases.english: he orders him to go round by the right-hand side of the hill until he found a way up that was less steep

phrases.latin: utque viam teneās nūllōque errōre trahāris
phrases.english: and even if you keep to the road and no wrong turning leads you astray
Let me; I’ll find the way myself.
Stay on the path, so you don’t get lost.

phrases.latin: puer aberrāvit inter hominēs ā patre.
phrases.english: the boy got separated from his father in the crowd.

sources: Lewis & Short: invenio · Lewis & Short: teneo
